The bronze bust of John Brown by Kansas sculptor Jim Brothers has the passion and movement of any Hellenistic masterpiece. Louis Copt’s painting of the Fox Creek Schoolhouse on the Kansas Tallgrass Prairie rivals the great Dutch master Johannes Vermeer’s “View of Delft.” The work of these fellow Midwesterners fires my imagination, inspires me, compels me to work harder, and pushes me to be a better teacher and writer.
Art is a catalyst in my life. It urges me from bed in the wee hours to plan a better way to convey some difficult concept to my students. It drives me to write, even when the words don’t come easily. Visual, literary, and musical art have pushed me to work and achieve my entire life. This has been especially true during the most trying times.
In the late ‘80s, fresh out of college, I started my first “real” job at an accounting firm, Laventhol & Horwath, in Philadelphia. Little did I know the firm was in dire straits. After eleven months I was laid off, and two months later the firm declared bankruptcy.
I was abruptly out of a job and unsure how I’d make rent. But I didn’t want friends or family to worry, so I kept my unemployment a secret.
In the morning, I dressed in a business suit like nothing was wrong and commuted to the Philadelphia Museum of Art, where I found solace. I absorbed the tranquility of the Japanese teahouse, and the sheer age of the medieval cloister put my short-term problems in perspective.
I sat with the work of great American painters. Among Thomas Eakins, Henry Ossawa Tanner, William Harnett, Charles Wilson Peale and others, I chose my next path. Their work renewed me, giving me the strength to carry on, the courage to decline opportunities in the corporate world, and the confidence to choose a more difficult road.
Soon I found a job at the University of Pennsylvania. My objective was to go back to school, and I knew the job provided tuition benefits. At Penn, once again, I found art to be my chief motivator. The fine arts library was designed in the nineteenth century by the great American architect Frank Furness. His masterpiece inspired me to keep going.
Every time the pressures of full-time work and graduate school made me want to drop out, I went to Furness’ library. I’d study in the main reading room for hours, and when fatigue set in, I needed only to look up at the vaulted ceiling, the strange American mix of Gothic and Romanesque influences, the terra-cotta, the leaded-glass windows ringed with maxims of encouragement and aphorisms like “Talkers are no great doers.”
Then I’d return to my books, sometimes studying through the night.
That inspiration helped carry me through my studies and eventually to graduate school at the University of Kansas.
Art drives us through adversity. It is the stimulus package we need in hard times. My own experience taught me that art can provide comfort, perspective and inspiration when we need them most. And that is why access to art matters.
Too many American political leaders think they’re projecting pragmatism when they treat art as an amenity, a luxury that we can indulge in only when times are good.

Six years ago, when Joe Klecker was named to the inaugural class of the On Athletics Club (OAC) in Boulder, Colorado, his goals were all about racing fast on the track. But based on his physiology, his tenacity, and even his genes, coach Dathan Ritzenhein already knew Klecker was destined to become a marathoner—and probably a very good one.
When the team now known as OAC Global formed in the summer of 2020, it featured eight postcollegiate runners chasing Olympic berths from 1,500 to 10,000 meters. The OAC sent several runners (including Klecker) to the Tokyo Olympics and brought home medals from Paris.
But track success was only the first step of what Ritzenhein envisioned. In the years since, he and coach Laura Thweatt have built an elite marathon program, too.
Kenyan great Hellen Obiri, four-time Major Marathon winner and current women’s New York City Marathon course record holder, put OAC on the marathon map after joining in 2022. The progression of Klecker (with a marathon PR of 2:05:56 from Boston), along with newer teammates Ryan Ford (2:05:46 marathon PR) and Patrick Kiprop (59:14 half marathon PR), has helped to solidify the team’s presence on the roads.
As all four prepare for the NYC Marathon, we went behind the curtain at the OAC Global Training Facility in Boulder to learn what has fueled their success.
1. Play Off Other Runners’ Strengths in Training
When On recruited Obiri to Boulder in 2022, the two-time Olympic silver medalist at 5,000 meters was about to move up to the marathon. That meant shifting from pure track speed and relatively low mileage (80 miles per week) to 120- to 125-mile weeks and grinding sessions like 25K tempo runs.
With no other marathoners on the team, she did portions of her long runs with 10,000-meter runner Alicia Monson and some longer tempo efforts and fartleks with Klecker. All three benefited.
Obiri became one of the best marathoners in the world, winning New York and Boston twice and an Olympic bronze medal in Paris; Monson broke the American 5,000- and 10,000-meter records in 2023, and Klecker got a taste of what marathon training was all about, which gave him proper perspective as he was about to begin his first marathon build.
“[Obiri’s] level is so high that, on a lot of our long runs and even some fartleks, we would overlap for a good chunk of those workouts,” Klecker, 29, tells Runner’s World. “And for me, it was harder than I thought. When you’re racing on the track, a long run is kind of a chill day because all of your hard work is on the track. But when you’d see her go out and do her long runs, she was just hammering from the start, and so I knew I really had to wrap my head around this new way of training for the roads.”
As Klecker got closer to his marathon debut last fall, the OAC signed Ford as his primary training partner. They developed a synergy, but weren’t entirely aligned in their schedules because Ford was building up to the Chicago Marathon and Klecker was preparing for New York a month later. But they did sync up for all of their training (including harder workouts) as they prepared for Boston, and that paid off with better racing execution and significant time drops.

The third quarter reversed that: net debt fell by more than $9 billion, and consensus has Exxon holding net cash by the end of 2027.

He said the company’s investments in production, refining capacity and global logistics positioned it to increase supply during the period.
“We recognize the impact high prices have on people’s lives and economic growth,” Woods said, adding that ExxonMobil has focused on growing “advantaged production” through commodity cycles.
Refining Operations and Gulf Coast Investments
Woods said ExxonMobil operated its fuels manufacturing facilities, excluding Middle East impacts, at its highest utilization level on record. The company ran about 3.6 million barrels of crude daily through its refineries and sold roughly 5.7 million barrels per day of gasoline, diesel and other finished products globally, he said.
Year to date, the company produced about 1.1 million barrels per day of diesel, according to Woods. He highlighted ExxonMobil’s 2023 Beaumont, Texas, expansion, a $2 billion project that added refining capacity equivalent to a medium-sized refinery. Woods said the investment paid for itself in roughly three years.
The company is pursuing additional U.S. Gulf Coast reconfiguration projects intended to raise distillate yield by about 100,000 barrels per day. The first phase is underway at Baytown, while additional work is planned at Baton Rouge and Beaumont to increase output of diesel, lubricants and chemical feedstocks.
Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer Neil Hansen said diesel yield was about 3.5% higher than in 2019. On a constant-margin basis, Hansen said volume and product-mix improvements combined with structural cost reductions have tripled underlying energy-products unit earnings since 2019.

Woods said the company aims to provide relatively consistent shareholder distributions across commodity cycles rather than increase commitments sharply during periods of high prices and retreat during weaker markets.
Hansen said ExxonMobil reduced net debt by more than $9 billion during the quarter. He said the company’s financial capacity enables it to maintain capital investment and shareholder distributions through different commodity-price environments.

Google zero, eventually, comes for us all.
That's the belief, and fear, that meaningful traffic from Google trends toward zero because of changes to its search engine practices and, more recently, its shift toward AI — answering people's search questions not with links to places like websites, but with AI summaries and chatbot dialogue.
Reddit's (RDDT) latest earnings report was a reckoning of Google's AI-led changes. And it underscored how Silicon Valley's full embrace of AI may come at the cost of huge swaths of the web — and the companies that rely on Google traffic to operate.
"People still want Reddit. It is just Google is not sending them to Reddit the way they used to," Steve Huffman, Reddit's co-founder and CEO, said on an earnings call earlier this week.
The company reported that search referral traffic was down meaningfully in the past quarter. Google's shift to AI mode and AI overviews has halted traffic that once flowed to the social forum.
Reddit stock fell 30% on Friday.
"Google is crawling us as hard as ever, so the demand hasn't changed from their point of view either," Huffman said. "The reality is the AI Mode does not drive traffic. Not for us, and not to anybody as far as I know."
The shift toward a more AI-inflicted internet isn't just hurting Reddit. It's hurting Google too, at least in the short term. Its parent company, Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL), shed almost $500 billion (or about two Netflixes) in market value after reporting a slowdown in its core search advertising business, in part due to the lower profitability of AI ads.
A critical view of the whole situation is that Google is smothering online publishers and sabotaging its own legacy business in its rush toward AI dominance.
But Reddit took a stance on the call that could be described as corporate Zen: "For AI Overviews and traffic, look, we don't control Google. We only control Reddit."
The company said it's not counting on that once-sweet Google traffic returning and plans to require all users to create Reddit accounts and sign in to access the site.
Other online publishers are looking to subscriptions to create direct relationships with audiences and are partnering with AI companies to ride the next wave of LLM-based media and product distribution.
Google, for its part, continues to argue the case (although not persuasively, given the stock plunge) that its AI efforts will prevail, even if it's still trying to figure out the problem of how to make more money with it.
Google executives no doubt disagree with the market sell-off, which has dragged the company's price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio back to levels not seen since 2012. Management knew this transition was coming. Their contention is that the success of AI tools will generate a new and different business model, and that it will be more profitable than the search-and-click paradigm the rest of the web relied on.
The bull case is that Google has good reasons to choose this bumpy path. But that also happens to be a bear case for almost everyone else.

Investing.com -- Goldman Sachs has warned that the sustainability of household demand for U.S. equities could become increasingly vulnerable to higher interest rates and the economic disruption associated with artificial intelligence. The brokerage has identified both as major uncertainties for equity valuations over the coming years.
The bank said household demand had become a critical pillar supporting the US stock market, with investors purchasing $840 billion of equities during the first half of 2026, more than offsetting weaker demand from US corporates.
Households directly own 42% of the US equity market and control a majority when indirect holdings through retirement accounts, mutual funds and ETFs are included.
However, Goldman said the trajectory of interest rates and the extent of AI-related disruption would rank among the most important determinants of how household allocations evolve.
Higher yields on cash and bonds can make equities less attractive, while the broader economic implications of AI remain an important source of uncertainty for long-term investment behaviour.
The risks come as household equity allocations have climbed to a record 55% of financial asset portfolios, alongside the strong performance of equities relative to other asset classes.
The concentration of ownership also presents an important consideration - the wealthiest 10% of households hold 87% of total household equity assets, making their investment decisions particularly influential.
Goldman's baseline forecasts remain supportive for 2027, assuming a stable labour market and modest declines in borrowing and market yields. The bank noted that equity fund flows have historically improved alongside rising household wealth, falling unemployment and reduced recession concerns.
Meanwhile, assets held in 401(k) plans have increased from 13% of the U.S. retirement market in 1995 to 21% currently, with younger participants allocating a greater proportion of their retirement balances to equities.
The demand outlook is becoming more consequential as corporate supply increases. U.S. public and private companies issued a net $175 billion of equity in the first half of 2026, while Goldman expects net public equity supply, including expiring lockups, to rise next year by its largest amount since 2000.

More strikes would keep product tight and margins wide, but a lasting ceasefire would let Middle East fuel move again and reduce the windfall.
Refining Is Where the War Money Landed
Exxon CEO Darren Woods said on the call that “roughly about half of Russia’s refining capacity has been taken offline” and that “1/3 of the shortage out there roughly is just the inability to get clean products out of the Middle East.”

France Wants a 5.5-Cent-per-Gigabyte Tax on Netflix, Google and Meta
France just voted to bill Netflix, Google, and Meta by the gigabyte, and the revenue estimate runs into the billions. Whether it survives the Senate and a potential White House response is another matter entirely.
On Friday, October 30, 2026, France’s National Assembly adopted amendment I-1358 to the 2027 finance bill. The amendment creates a tax of €0.055, or 5.5 euro cents (about 6.1 U.S. cents), on every gigabyte that content providers send to subscribers of French internet providers. It passed 11 to 10, with only 35 of the Assembly’s 577 deputies taking part.
Socialist deputy Laurent Lhardit’s amendment carried over the objections of the government and the budget’s general rapporteur. Socialist, LFI, Ecologist, and GDR deputies voted yes, and the finance committee had already turned down the same idea earlier in October.
Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX | NFLX Price Prediction) closed at $62.08, up 0.05%. Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG, NASDAQ:GOOGL) fell 1.4% to $279.84, and Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) slipped 1.53% to $614.99. None of those moves link to the vote.
What Amendment I-1358 Actually Does
The tax falls on the companies sending the data. Internet providers only measure the amounts under the telecom regulator Arcep and the tax administration, and traffic routed through content delivery networks is counted as it leaves those networks.
Each company’s bill is capped at 15% of its French revenue or 2% of its worldwide revenue, with no separate size threshold. Detailed rules would be set later by decree.
The explanatory statement says Google, Meta, Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Netflix and Akamai (NASDAQ:AKAM) carry half the traffic Arcep measures, out of 200 billion gigabytes a year. It adds: “Au taux de 0,055 € par giga, un rendement de 10 Md€ est attendu.” That yield of about $11.2 billion is Lhardit’s own estimate, and the administration has yet to assess it. The companies appear only in that statement, because the tax itself applies to any content provider.
Who Would Actually Feel the Bill
Netflix sells only video, so its traffic is heavy relative to its revenue, and the French revenue cap would likely set its bill. EMEA brought in $4.11 billion of Netflix’s third-quarter revenue, which makes Europe material even though France is only one market within it.
Alphabet carries YouTube, but search ads produce most of its revenue and very little traffic. Against third-quarter revenue of $127.58 billion, any French bill would be small. Meta carries video across its apps, and general rapporteur Philippe Juvin warned that the big platforms could pass the cost on to advertisers.
Public Accounts Minister David Amiel wondered whether the tax would work at all. He estimated that about half the yield could fall on smaller content providers, including French ones.

A one-vote margin in a nearly empty chamber carries little weight. The Senate still has to take up the bill, and the government can force a budget through without a vote under Article 49, paragraph 3, which could produce a final text that drops this amendment.

Investing.com -- Taiwan is emerging as the biggest domestic beneficiary of Asia's artificial intelligence export boom, followed by South Korea, as stronger technology demand boosts economic activity, government revenues and investment, according to Bank of America.
The bank said AI-related exports have become a major growth driver for Taiwan, South Korea and China, although the economic benefits are spreading unevenly across the three markets.
Year-to-date exports have increased 57% year over year in South Korea, 44% in Taiwan and 21% in China, according to BofA's analysis.
Despite South Korea recording the strongest export growth, Taiwan is expected to experience the largest domestic spillover effects.
BofA attributed the differences to the relative size of each economy's technology sector, production capacity constraints and broader economic conditions.
Taiwan's substantial exposure to technology manufacturing means stronger external demand can translate into wider domestic economic gains.
South Korea also stands to benefit significantly, with the export expansion supporting domestic activity and government finances.
China is benefiting from stronger technology exports, but weaker domestic demand and economic headwinds are limiting the broader impact.
The differences are also shaping fiscal policy across the region.
BofA said rising exports have increased government tax revenues in all three economies, creating opportunities for additional public spending.
In Taiwan and South Korea, higher fiscal receipts are helping finance transfers and investment, providing another channel through which export growth supports domestic demand.
China has not experienced a comparable spending boost, partly reflecting financial constraints facing local governments.
The uneven economic effects are expected to produce different monetary policy responses.
In Taiwan and South Korea, stronger domestic demand and positive output gaps are adding to inflationary pressures, supporting the case for further interest rate increases.
China faces a different outlook, with softer domestic demand pointing toward additional monetary easing.
BofA's assessment suggests Taiwan and South Korea are positioned to capture stronger economy-wide benefits from the AI boom, with China's gains remaining more concentrated amid domestic challenges.

Lackluster earnings from Alphabet (GOOG), Amazon (AMZN), Intel (INTC) sent the tech complex into a steep sell-off, ending a wild week that began with Anthropic's S-1 filing.

On Tuesday, our focus shifts to politics, as US midterms are set to influence everything from control of Congress and the Iran war to the data center boom. On top of that, AMD (AMD) and Marathon Petroleum Corporation (MPC) both report earnings, and the US government will report JOLTS data in the first major labor market update of the week.
Wednesday and Thursday bring earnings from Toyota Motor (TM), ConocoPhillips (COP), Eaton Corporation (ETN), Arm Holdings (ARM), McDonald's (MCD), and a range of other corporate market heavyweights, alongside a smattering of economic data.
And all of that excitement sets up Friday's October nonfarm payrolls report, the banner data release of the week.
Big Tech's sell-off wasn't about the actual fundamentals
It was a deeply red week for the tech sector after a slew of earnings failed to give investors the signs of strength they were looking (and hoping) for.
At Alphabet, a miss on both revenue and profit sent shares falling 13% as Sundar Pichai said that while the company's search division had grown, the money wasn't keeping up as AI cuts into search monetization.
Down the street at Amazon, a double miss on both earnings and revenue triggered a sell-off that couldn't be stopped by strong cloud growth in AWS.

Intel's data center and AI segment pulled down $7.318 billion against estimates of $6.675 billion expected, marking 78% growth year on year, while Sandisk (SNDK) beat on both the top and bottom lines yet still got pulled into a sell-off.

It’s been a long and winding journey for Zouhair Talbi to realize his American dream, but winning the Houston Marathon in 2:05.45 on January 11 as a U.S. citizen was only part of that dream coming true.
The 31-year-old Moroccan-born runner ran the third-fastest time ever by a U.S. runner on a record-eligible course—behind only American record holder Conner Mantz (2:04:43 in Chicago last fall) and Khalid Khannouchi (2:05:38 in London in 2002)—taking nearly a minute off his personal best set two years earlier in Houston when he ran under his Moroccan citizenship in his lead-up to the Paris Olympics.
But not long after he celebrated at the finish line with an American flag draped over his shoulders, Zouhair relished another milestone moment as his wife, Elizabeth Talbi, 23, also had a breakthrough result in the marathon, placing 10th among women in 2:35:26—a 15-minute personal best from her debut effort in 2024—just 10 months after giving birth to their son, Amir.
Moreover, they each surpassed the qualifying standards for the 2028 U.S. Olympic Trials Marathon, which means they’ll both be on the starting line of the races that will determine who will make the U.S. team for the Los Angeles Olympics. The race will either be in Phoenix or St. Louis, and it is tentatively scheduled for the weekend of March 25-26, 2028. In other words, after August 2027, when Zouhair becomes eligible to officially compete for the U.S. in international races and national team qualifying events.
Best of all, they were also able to celebrate their success with Amir, who was cared for during the race by Elizabeth’s sister, Kaitlyn, who lives in Houston.
“It was a special day,” Zouhair said. “It was the first time I was listed as a U.S. runner with the American flag next to my name. It was something I had always dreamed of when I thought about coming to America. And to have Elizabeth run so well, too, really made it a special day for both of us.”

ExxonMobil (XOM +2.16%) just raised its quarterly dividend by another 3.9%, extending its growth streak to an industry-leading 44 consecutive years. That's a longer streak than 95% of companies in the S&P 500.
However, it was a very modest raise compared to its free cash flow, which has surged 90% year-over-year to $39 billion over the last nine months. That gap between the modest dividend increase and surging free cash flow isn't an accident, and what it says about how Exxon runs its cash is worth a closer look.
Image source: Getty Images.
Focused on the long term
ExxonMobil generated $19.1 billion in free cash flow during the third quarter alone, nearly as much as it produced during the first nine months of last year ($20.6 billion). That's enough cash to cover a year's worth of dividends with room to spare ($17.2 billion annually at its current $4.3 billion quarterly run rate). Clearly, Exxon has the capacity to deliver a much higher dividend increase.
However, the company's dividend payment is a fixed expense. Its cash flow, on the other hand, is highly variable. It has surged this year due to higher oil prices and refining margins caused by supply disruptions in the Middle East. When those disruptions finally ease, pricing and margins will fall, as will Exxon's free cash flow.

But what you do in the hours and days immediately following 26.2 miles can determine how quickly you bounce back—not only physically but also how soon you’ll feel emotionally ready to get moving again. Marathons are draining, and that finish-line euphoria won’t keep sustaining you through continuous daily runs if you don’t let yourself recover fully.
After conquering 14 marathon finish lines in all seasons and a few back-to-back marathons too, I’ve learned a few key lessons about how to successfully get back to running postrace. Keep these in mind if you’ve just crossed a marathon off your list and want to lace up your running shoes again soon.
Don’t: Kick your feet up the entire rest of race day.
The first time I ran the New York City Marathon, I lived in a fifth-floor walk-up apartment on the Upper East Side. Going down those stairs the next day was excruciating, but I went outside anyway and went for a walk—and my legs felt immensely better a day later, compared with when I didn’t take those steps after other races.
Obviously, you should give yourself some downtime and relax after a marathon, but when I make a point to walk around more often right after a race and to do some other light activity (like easy pedaling on my Peloton) over the following few days, it always helps my legs feel way better sooner. Sitting on the couch all day will only increase your stiffness.
Do: Treat yourself!
Regardless of whether you hit a PR, qualified for Boston, or barely made it over the finish line, completing a marathon is a big accomplishment. I’ve found that taking some time after 26.2 to celebrate and appreciate my body for what it can do—and my mind for what it can push through—is an important step before jumping right back into running. When I push ahead without taking joy and pride in what I achieved, I wind up feeling run down and unmotivated.
If you feel like having a decadent meal and celebratory beers as part of that acknowledgment, Jeff Gaudette, owner and head coach at RunnersConnect, says go for it! But to feel up to running again soon, have something nutritious first.
“The focus on recovery needs to be more dialed in if you're going to do another race soon,” he says. “That means nutrition and refueling a little more diligently. You can still enjoy pizza and beer, but make sure you get some protein and healthy carbs beforehand.”
Research backs this nutrient combo up: One 2018 study in Nutrients found that eating both carbs and protein immediately postrace helped marathoners’ physical fatigue, mental energy, and soreness improve within three days compared with those who ate carbs alone.

She’s been on two Olympic teams and won the Boston Marathon, but Des Linden is still a rookie when it comes to ultra events.
In her first 100-miler, the Javelina Jundred on October 31 (stretching into November 1 for some runners) in Fountain Hills, Arizona, Linden finished as the ninth woman in 16 hours and 58 minutes.
Linden ran strongly for the first three laps of the five-lap race. She took over the lead at about the 40-mile mark and held onto that lead for the next 20 miles.
She hit 60.3 miles at 8:01:12, an average of 7:58 per mile pace for more than twice the marathon distance over the hilly trails.
But at the aid station at 60.3 miles, Linden sat down while her crew tended to her. She changed shoes and took about five minutes to get up and start running again. Within a half a mile of leaving the aid station, she was walking, and two female runners, Katie Asmuth and Carla Molinaro, passed her.
The final 40 miles took her 8 hours and 57 minutes.
Although the daylight hours were primarily dry on the desert loop, heavy rain drenched the course at the start and after night fell, drawing comparisons to the 2018 Boston Marathon, which Linden won, in a nor’easter.
The women’s race was incredibly close.
Heather Jackson, 42, won in 13:48:29, averaging 8:17 pace. Molinaro was second in 13:49:24, after Jackson overtook her in the final quarter mile of the race. Both earned “golden tickets” for the Western States Endurance Run, the famed 100-miler in June that goes from Olympic Valley to Auburn, California.
The men’s race was also close: Rob Molke, 35, finished in 12:11:30, holding off Noah Dusseau, who was runner-up in 12:12:57. They also earned “golden tickets” for Western States.
Linden will likely be motivated to solve the puzzle of the 100-mile distance, as she was early in her marathon career when she wanted to master 26.2 miles.
Her training wasn’t ideal leading up to Javelina, although she had several two-day stretches when she ran 30 miles one day and 20 the next.
She was aware she would need to adjust her goals if she started to struggle in the later miles.
“Just get to the finish. I think that’s super important,” she said in a phone interview with Runner’s World on October 29. “I think if I can run the whole time, that’s going to be great. And then if it’s going really well, I would love to get a golden ticket. But those are just as flexible as the plan. I know that even finishing can be something that all of a sudden comes into question. It’s just so different from anything I've done.”
Linden was also looking forward to the relaxed vibe and the chance to be around her crew and other runners.
“As a runner, you make these friends and they become your community,” she said. “But everyone lives [all over] the country. It’s hard to meet up with people, and so this is really just an excuse to hang out with a bunch of people who are really fun. It’ll be good. A good hang, no matter what.”

Binance began restoring customer withdrawals Sunday after hackers drained over $6 billion in the biggest cyber theft ever recorded, as the crypto industry awaits answers on the breach blamed on North Korea and steps to strengthen the exchange’s defenses.
The world’s largest digital-asset platform reopened Bitcoin withdrawals after 2 p.m. Singapore time, more than two days after halting them following the breach. By evening in Asia, the exchange had seen some $3.5 billion in net outflows, according to DefiLlama data. Co-Chief Executive Officer Yi He said on X some transfers are between Binance wallets.
The first phase of withdrawals covers 15 tokens, including Ether and the two biggest stablecoins, Tether’s USDT and Circle Internet Group Inc.’s USDC, Binance said on X. Withdrawals on 15 blockchain networks including Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain, XRP and Base resumed by around 8:30 p.m. in Singapore, according to the company.
Read more: Binance’s $6.3 Billion Hack: How Crypto Insurance Works
Binance dwarfs its industry rivals, with roughly $132 billion in assets, compared with about $29 billion at the second-largest exchange OKX. “We are taking a phased approach by prioritizing tokens based on the past week data of user demand, so that each network and asset pair can be restored carefully, with stability and security checks completed before access is reopened,” Binance said.
Quantitative trading firm SQS Trading has about a quarter of its trading capital on Binance, and is cutting that by roughly a third, according to founder Eli Williams, who added that it won’t flatten positions or reduce usage of the exchange as a venue for hedging. “It’s hard to forecast what the net impact will be at this point but we will be monitoring capital outflows and volume impact relative to other major venues,” Williams said.
Others are holding off any changes. Justin d’Anethan, head of research at Arctic Digital, a private markets advisory firm, said he’s not fazed by the hack. “When something seems fishy, it’s good to act fast; but when something catastrophic happens, it’s better to hold off doing anything,” he said. “I haven’t and wouldn’t move away from Binance.”
A spokesperson for Binance said the withdrawal volumes “spiked at the beginning,” but are now stabilizing to what the company considers normal activity, and a small percentage of its overall assets under management.
The restart tests Binance’s promise to make customers whole following a theft four times the size of the previous record crypto hack at Bybit in 2025. The US Federal Bureau of Investigation said on Saturday the Binance attack was carried out by TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit it also held responsible for the roughly $1.5 billion Bybit theft.
The market fallout appears relatively contained, with most major cryptocurrencies seeing a change of less than 1% Sunday. Bitcoin, which accounts for about 60% of the sector’s market value, was trading around $78,000, about 5% below its Thursday high before the attack.
“On some level, this shows how much the industry has matured,” said Haseeb Qureshi, managing partner at venture fund Dragonfly. “We saw extraordinarily quick responses.”
Binance said it has so far replaced about 95% of the stolen cryptocurrency using its corporate treasury, emergency funds and insurance funds. The funds drained in the attack were a mix of the largest cryptocurrencies across 10 blockchains, including Bitcoin and Ethereum.
